title: Observer Pattern
summary: Notifying many dependents when one object's state changes, without hard-wiring the subject to every listener that cares.

slides.markdown:
**Observer** lets one object (the subject) broadcast state changes to any number of interested objects (observers) without knowing who they are ahead of time. A stock ticker updates one price; a dozen unrelated widgets — a chart, a portfolio total, a price alert — all need to react.

Instead of the ticker calling `chart.update()`, `portfolio.update()`, `alert.check()` by name, observers register themselves and the subject just says "something changed" to whoever's listening. This is the pattern behind pub/sub, UI event listeners, and reactive streams.

slides.sectionTitle: The problem: notifying many dependents when one object's state changes
slides.markdown:
A `StockPrice` object updates every time a trade executes. Three unrelated parts of the app need to know: a `PriceChart` redraws, a `PortfolioValue` recalculates, a `PriceAlert` checks a threshold. The naive fix is `StockPrice` holding direct references to all three and calling their update methods by name.

That breaks the moment a fourth dependent shows up — you're back inside `StockPrice`, adding another hardcoded call, and `StockPrice` now imports and knows about UI components it has no business knowing about. Worse, dependents can't be added or removed at runtime without editing the subject.

The underlying problem: one object's change needs to reach an open-ended, changing set of dependents, without the subject hardcoding who they are.

slides.sectionTitle: Observer: a subject maintains a list of observers and pushes/pulls updates
slides.markdown:
The **subject** exposes `subscribe(observer)` and `unsubscribe(observer)` and keeps an internal list. When its state changes, it loops over that list and calls a single shared method on each — `notify(newState)` or `update()` — without knowing or caring what any observer actually does with it.

Observers implement one interface — say `PriceObserver` with `onPriceChanged(price)` — and register themselves. `StockPrice` never imports `PriceChart` or `PortfolioValue` by name; it only knows the `PriceObserver` interface.

Adding a fourth dependent means it calls `subscribe()` on itself — `StockPrice` doesn't change at all.

slides.sectionTitle: Diagram: subject fan-out to multiple observers
slides.markdown:
A `Subject` holds a list of registered `Observer` references. On a state change it iterates that list once, calling the same `update()` method on each — one event, many independent reactions, no observer aware of the others.

![A Subject fanning out update() calls to three Observer boxes: Chart, PortfolioValue, PriceAlert](assets/observer-fanout.svg)

The fan-out is one-directional and synchronous by default: the subject doesn't proceed past `notify()` until every observer's `update()` returns (unless you deliberately make it async).

slides.sectionTitle: Code: a stock-price subject notifying multiple display observers
Compare: push vs pull observer models
slides.markdown:
| | Push model | Pull model |
|---|---|---|
| What the subject sends | The new data itself — `onPriceChanged(191.20)` | Just a signal — `onChanged()`, no data |
| What the observer does | Uses the data directly | Calls back into the subject — `subject.getPrice()` — to fetch what it needs |
| Coupling | Observer interface tied to the subject's data shape | Looser — observer only needs a reference to the subject |
| Waste | None — exact data sent every time | Observer may fetch more than it needs, or fetch when it didn't need to |

**How to decide:** push when there's one obvious piece of data every observer wants (the new price); pull when different observers need different subsets of subject state, so a fixed push payload would either under- or over-serve them.

slides.sectionTitle: Pitfall: memory leaks from observers that never unsubscribe
slides.markdown:
**Wrong belief:** "Once I `subscribe()`, I'm done — the framework will clean it up."

**Why it's wrong:** the subject holds a live reference to every observer in its list. If a `PriceChart` component gets destroyed (a user navigates away) but never calls `unsubscribe()`, `StockPrice` still holds a reference to it — the garbage collector can't reclaim it, and every future `setPrice()` still calls `update()` on a widget nobody can see. This is one of the most common real-world memory leaks in event-driven UIs.

**Correct model:** every `subscribe()` needs a matching `unsubscribe()` tied to the observer's own lifecycle — a component's teardown/destroy hook, not an afterthought. Some frameworks return an unsubscribe function from `subscribe()` specifically to make this hard to forget.

slides.sectionTitle: Pitfall: notification-order dependencies — an observer that mutates the subject mid-notify
slides.markdown:
**Wrong belief:** "Observers are independent, so it doesn't matter what order they run in or what they do inside `update()`."

**Why it's wrong:** if `PriceAlert.onPriceChanged()` calls back into `StockPrice.setPrice()` (say, to apply a correction), it can trigger a second `notify()` loop while the first is still iterating — observers further down the original list now see a different price than the ones before them, or the list itself changes mid-iteration if an observer subscribes/unsubscribes from inside `update()`.

**Correct model:** treat observer callbacks as read-only reactions, not places to mutate the subject. If a reaction must eventually change the subject's state, queue it for after the current notification finishes, not inline.

slides.sectionTitle: Where this shows up: pub/sub, UI event listeners, reactive streams
slides.markdown:
Observer is everywhere once you know the shape. **UI frameworks**: `addEventListener('click', handler)` is a subject (the DOM node) with a list of observers (handlers) called on an event. **Pub/sub systems** like Kafka or Redis Pub/Sub are Observer at a distributed scale — a topic is the subject, consumers are observers, and the broker handles the fan-out. **Reactive streams** (RxJS `Observable`, Kotlin `Flow`) formalize push-based Observer with operators for filtering and combining streams of updates.

Recognizing this lets you reuse Observer's known failure modes — unsubscribe discipline, notification-order bugs — even when the library hides the pattern's name.
